opus-5.5.text:
I think one of the most exciting things is that language models give us something linguists have never really had: a learner we can actually experiment on. For decades, a lot of the big debates about language, like how much of our linguistic ability is innate versus learned from input, were argued mostly through theory, because you can't ethically raise a child on a strange, made-up language just to see what happens. With language models, you can. You control the training data completely, and you can watch what the system learns and what it struggles with.

That was a big motivation for our work on "impossible languages." There's been a strong claim, associated with Chomsky and others, that large language models are equally capable of learning possible and impossible human languages, and so they can't tell us anything about human language. We thought that was an empirical claim we could test. So we built synthetic languages by systematically perturbing English: shuffling word order, reversing sentences, or introducing grammar rules that depend on counting word positions instead of on hierarchical structure, which human languages don't seem to do. Then we trained GPT-2-style models on them and compared how well they learned each one.

We found that the models did *not* learn everything equally well. They had a much harder time with the more unnatural languages, especially the ones that broke the kind of locality and structure that real languages have. That doesn't mean a transformer is a model of the human brain, and I'm careful not to overclaim. But it suggests these models have inductive biases that partially line up with properties of human languages. Once you accept that, they become a tool for asking finer-grained questions: which architectural biases matter, how much data you need, and which properties of language are learnable from exposure alone.

The other side of my work, on tokenization and byte-level models, connects to this too. Most models see text through a tokenizer that someone designed by hand, which is a strong assumption about what the units of language are. If models can learn useful units directly from raw characters or bytes, that raises questions about how structure emerges from the signal itself, which is very close to the questions linguists ask about how children segment speech.

So I see language models less as a replacement for linguistic theory and more as a new kind of experimental lab. They let us turn longstanding philosophical arguments into experiments, and I think that will be really productive for both NLP and linguistics.

r001.rationale: The response presents language models as experimental tools for investigating human language, but it does not clearly contrast that use with using them to imitate human language.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks so much for having me. I think the biggest shift is that language models give us a kind of experimental subject we've never had before. For a long time, if you wanted to ask "what kinds of structure can a learner pick up from exposure to language alone," you were stuck with humans, and humans come with a lot of baggage. You can't rerun a child's acquisition with a different input, you can't give them a language that violates some property you care about, and you can't peer inside the whole system while it's learning. With a model, you can.

So a lot of my work has been about using models almost like a controlled lab. One line of that is the "impossible languages" work, where we take English and systematically mess with it in ways no human language does. We shuffle words, we reverse chunks of sentences, we add a rule like "put a verb marker after the fourth word" that's keyed to counting positions rather than to syntactic structure. Then we train models from scratch on each variant and ask: does the model learn these equally well? If language models were truly indifferent to the structure of what they learn, you'd expect roughly the same learning curves across the board. What we actually see is that the more unnatural the language, the harder it is for the model, and the ordering tracks linguistic intuitions pretty closely. That lets you start separating out which aspects of human language are hard because of something about the learner versus something about the input, which is a question linguists have argued over for decades without a good way to test it.

The other side of it is that models force you to be precise about your questions. A claim like "language has hierarchical structure" is easy to say. But when you have to turn it into a training manipulation, or into a probe you can run on a network, you discover all the places where the claim was underspecified. I find that discipline really productive. It doesn't replace theoretical linguistics or psycholinguistics, but it adds a third kind of evidence.

And the thing I'd push back on is the idea that the models have to be good cognitive models of humans for this to be useful. They clearly aren't in many respects; they see orders of magnitude more data than a child, and they don't learn through interaction. But that's actually fine for a lot of questions. If even a system with those advantages struggles with certain structures, that tells you something about the structures. And if it succeeds where theory predicted it shouldn't, that's interesting too, because now you have to figure out what signal it found. Either way you've learned something about language, not just about the model.

r001.rationale: The response presents language models as controlled experimental tools for learning about language, and says they need not be good cognitive models of humans to be useful. This distinguishes their research use from using them to reproduce human cognition or language behavior.

astra-6.text:
I think language models give us a new way to test hypotheses about why human language looks the way it does. We observe patterns across languages, but it’s difficult to determine whether those patterns reflect something specific to human cognition or whether they emerge from learning and using language more generally.

With a language model, we can manipulate the training data and ask, what happens if we change a particular property of language? Can the model still learn it? For example, we can construct languages that violate patterns we typically see in human languages and compare how easily models learn those with how easily they learn natural language.

The challenge is interpreting that comparison. A model learning something doesn’t mean a human could learn it, or that they would learn it in the same way. But it gives us a controlled setting for making our hypotheses more precise—and for asking what additional constraints we need to explain human language.

r001.rationale: The response clearly describes using language models as tools to test hypotheses about human language, but it does not distinguish that use from using them to imitate human language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language models give us a new way to test hypotheses about why human language looks the way it does. We can observe patterns across languages, but observation alone doesn’t necessarily tell us what causes those patterns. Is it something about our learning mechanisms, the data we encounter, or the pressures of communication?

With a language model, we can manipulate the learning environment. We can change the training data, introduce a particular linguistic rule, and ask whether the model can learn it. That lets us explore counterfactuals: What if language worked differently? Would it still be learnable?

The challenge is connecting those results back to humans. A model learning something doesn’t establish that a child could learn it in the same way. But it gives us a controlled setting for making our hypotheses more precise and figuring out what evidence would distinguish them.

r001.rationale: The response presents language models as controlled tools for testing hypotheses about human language, but it never contrasts that use with using them to imitate human language.
